title: Type 2 history: close the old row, add the new one
objective_text: Apply a batch of customer changes to a dimension that keeps history for city (type 2) and overwrites email (type 1).
scenario: Finance reports revenue by the city a customer lived in when they ordered, so city changes must keep history. Marketing only ever wants the latest email address, on every row. Tonight's batch has a move, an email change, a customer with no change and a new customer.
verifies: Your statements ran on this PC with DuckDB and left dim_customer with the expected history.
Every customer has exactly one current row and every surrogate key is unique.
does_not_verify: That the statements run in a Fabric Warehouse or Spark SQL unchanged: UPDATE ... FROM is written differently in Spark SQL, where MERGE is the usual way.
Behaviour under concurrent loads, which needs the target's own transaction rules.

expected.result: The starter's final SELECT over dim_customer, ordered by customer_key.

validation.pass: History and current rows are right.
validation.fail: Check each customer in customer_changes: which ones need a new row, and which rows need the new email?

validation.pass: Keys are unique and every row has its dates.
validation.fail: A key appears twice or a row is missing valid_from or is_current.

hints: There are three kinds of change: email (overwrite every row of the customer), city (close the current row and add a new one), and a new customer (add a row).
Do the type 1 email update first, on all of the customer's rows, so the new type 2 row and the old ones agree.
New keys continue from max(customer_key); row_number() OVER (ORDER BY customer_id) numbers the rows you insert.
explanation: A type 2 attribute keeps the past: the current row is closed (valid_to set, is_current false) and a new row with a new surrogate key starts on the change date, so old facts keep pointing at the old city. A type 1 attribute is corrected everywhere, including closed rows, because nobody needs the old value. Mixing the two in one dimension is common; the order of the steps decides whether the new row carries the new email.
